title: H-1B Workers Are Giving Up on US Tech Jobs as Fees and Delays Pile Up
excerpt: Bloomberg profiles a Google engineer leaving for the UK on a Global Talent visa, and reports employers from IBM to Flywire rethinking US sponsorship as new charges and PERM suspensions stack up.
body:
• Bloomberg profiles Yash Sharma, a 36-year-old Google software engineer from India who is leaving the US for the United Kingdom next month after six years on an H-1B visa, with a UK Global Talent visa that needs no job offer.
  • The departures follow a stack of changes: a $100,000 charge on some overseas H-1B hires (halted by a court), a different $103,000 charge on new applications announced in August, and suspensions of major employers from the PERM green card programme.
  • The US issued roughly 260,000 fewer short-term non-immigrant visas in the 2025 budget year than the year before, Bloomberg reported, citing Migration Policy Institute analysis of federal data.
  • For readers whose employers sponsor green cards: the Labor Department's proposed overhaul of the PERM programme is open for public comment through January 19, 2027.

Yash Sharma decided last month that he has had enough of the US. The 36-year-old Google software engineer from India has held an H-1B visa for six years, and he told Bloomberg that halfway through Donald Trump's second term, the constant rule changes around visas for highly skilled immigrants, the unknowns they create and the slim odds of becoming a citizen have all become too much.

Sharma loves his life in San Francisco and working at the epicentre of tech and AI, Bloomberg reported, but feels he has run out of options to gain permanent residency and build a life there. The United Kingdom has approved him for a Global Talent visa that lets him move without a job offer, according to Bloomberg's reporting summarised by Quartz. His application for a US extraordinary-ability visa was turned down after a lengthy wait, and he has avoided travelling abroad for the past 18 months out of concern that he would not be allowed back in. He told Bloomberg the US feels like a "golden prison."

Who is affected

The workers in Bloomberg's reporting are highly skilled immigrants already in the US on temporary visas — H-1B holders in tech jobs, a group in which Indians are the largest nationality — together with the employers who sponsor them for visas and green cards. Nothing in the reported changes cancels the status of people already holding valid visas. What has changed is the cost and predictability of staying: new fees on applications, longer and less certain paths to permanent residency, and employers pulling back from sponsorship altogether.

A stack of changes, not one

The administration began with a proclamation demanding $100,000 for some would-be employees living abroad; a court halted that payment, and the administration then announced a different $103,000 charge on new H-1B applications in August, Bloomberg reported. Last month, the Labor Department barred Microsoft, Adobe and a set of large IT outsourcing companies from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme — the employer-sponsored first step toward most employment-based green cards — because of ongoing federal investigations, according to Bloomberg; Deputy Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions.

This week the department went further, proposing the first comprehensive reforms to the PERM programme in nearly 20 years. The proposed rule would strengthen recruitment standards and recordkeeping requirements and eliminate administrative exemptions to the labour market test, the agency said, and comments are open through January 19, 2027.

Companies are moving, too

IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its largest division; affected workers can either continue with IBM from a location abroad or leave the firm before the year ends, Bloomberg reported. Boston-based Flywire disclosed in its quarterly report this month that it is considering shifting hiring and product development to cheaper locations to absorb rising H-1B visa expenses. Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart, told Bloomberg some corporate clients are saying "it's too much, it's time to start offshoring."

"We are creating a brain drain."

— Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel, American Immigration Lawyers Association, to Bloomberg

The numbers behind the mood

The US handed out roughly 260,000 fewer short-term, non-immigrant visas in the 2025 budget year compared with the previous one, according to Bloomberg, citing Migration Policy Institute analysis of federal data — a year that still included the final three complete months of former President Joe Biden's time in office. New foreign student enrolment at US universities is down an estimated 15 per cent this fall, Bloomberg reported, citing the Institute of International Education. The administration contends employers and workers have exploited the immigration system, depressing wages for Americans.

What to do next

If you hold an H-1B, none of the reported measures changes your current status, and Sharma's story is a decision, not a requirement. The concrete open item is the PERM proposal: employers and workers who rely on the programme can file comments on the Labor Department's proposed rule through January 19, 2027. Workers weighing an exit now have a worked example in Bloomberg's reporting — the UK Global Talent route Sharma used requires no job offer — and anyone whose employer has been suspended from PERM should ask their immigration counsel what the suspension does to a pending case, because the reporting does not settle that question.
